_note: The European Portuguese pronunciation rules in the right-hand column of /pronunciation (AusspracheRegeln.astro), in teaching order. `match` is a regular expression tested on the lower-case word without an article: if it matches, the rule is listed under “For this word”. A rule without `match` is general and is never highlighted. `mark` (optional) is the stressed syllable, shown in bold. Standard Portuguese of Portugal (Lisbon); what Brazil does differently is in `ptBR`. Rule ids are the old slot ids (content-plan §1.3) plus aberta-fechada, nasal, ao and x. Phonetic descriptions are simplified for learners; sound values to verify against a pronunciation dictionary (Infopédia, Priberam). Not yet reviewed by a teacher.

ptBR.note: In Brazil unstressed vowels are fuller: pequeno is “pekeno”, and t and d before i are said ch and j: tia, dia.

rules.title: Weak vowels: the unstressed e nearly disappears
rules.text: This is the biggest difference from Spanish or Italian. In Portugal, vowels that are not stressed become weak and short. An unstressed e is a very short, closed sound (like the e in “roses”) or is not said at all: pequeno sounds like “p'keno”, telefone like “t'lefon'”. A final e is hardly heard: leite, noite. An unstressed a is a short, relaxed “uh” (casa), and a final unstressed o sounds like u (livro is “livru”). Listeners understand you if you say full vowels, but you will sound foreign, and you will not understand fast speech until you know that the consonants carry the word.

examples.note: p'keno: the first e almost disappears
t'lefon': first and last e are weak
'studar: the first e is nearly lost

rules.title: Open and closed vowels: é, ê, ó, ô
rules.text: Stressed e and o can be open or closed. The accent tells you: é and ó are open (mouth wide, like the vowels of “bed” and “not”), ê and ô are closed (lips rounder, like the vowels of French “fée” and “beau”). A single wrong vowel can change the word: avó is grandmother, avô is grandfather; pode (he can) is not pôde (he could). Without an accent the vowel has to be learned with the word, but a few patterns help: the plural of some words opens the vowel (o ovo, os ovos; o olho, os olhos), and e or o before m or n (nasal) are closed (tema, homem).

examples.note: open o in the plural; ovo has a closed o

rules.title: Nasal vowels
rules.text: A vowel before m or n at the end of a syllable (and a vowel with a tilde) is nasal: air goes through your nose and the m or n is not a separate sound. Compare “bom” with English “bone”: the vowel is nasal and you do not finish with a clear n. Nasal vowels also exist in French (bon, vin), so they are not new to French speakers, but the Portuguese ones are different: Portuguese em is closer to “ãy”, and a nasal a is a weak “ã”. Before a vowel there is no nasalisation: ano and cama have a clear n or m, because the n or m begins the next syllable.

examples.note: even without n or m: the ui is nasal

rules.title: ão, ãe, õe: nasal diphthongs
rules.text: Three endings are very frequent and a nasal glide: ão (pão, são, coração), ãe (mãe, cães) and õe (põe, limões). Start with the nasal vowel and let it glide on to a short w (ão) or y (ãe, õe). You do not say a clear n at the end. Think “pãw”, “mãy”, “põy”. The plural of -ão words is usually -ões (um limão, dois limões), and the ending of many words in -ção is the same sound: informação, estação.

rules.title: Two vowels together: diphthongs
rules.text: When i or u stands next to another vowel, the two normally form one syllable (a diphthong): pai, leite, pouco, muito, eu. The second vowel is short. In Portugal, ei is a short “ɐy” (like “ay” with a relaxed start) and ou is just o: pouco is “poco”. A written accent on the i or u splits the two vowels into separate syllables: país is pa-ís, saída is sa-í-da. Many Portuguese words have two vowels together that are not a diphthong, such as ia in dia and ea in área: here the vowels are two syllables or a very quick glide.

rules.title: Word stress: which syllable is strong?
rules.text: Every word has one strong syllable, and the rules are simple. A word that ends in a, e, o, as, es, os, am, em or ens is stressed on the second-to-last syllable. A word that ends in i, u, l, r, z, im, um or a nasal ã/ão is stressed on the last syllable. Where a word breaks these rules, it has a written accent. Because the stress is so strong, the unstressed vowels become weak (see the first rule).

rules.title: Written accents
rules.text: There are four marks. The acute (á, é, í, ó, ú) shows the stressed syllable and an open vowel. The circumflex (â, ê, ô) shows the stressed syllable and a closed vowel. The tilde (ã, õ) shows a nasal vowel. The grave (à) is only used when a and a join: vou à praia. Words stressed three syllables from the end always have an accent: médico, música, último. An accent can change the word: está (is) and esta (this), país (country) and pais (parents), falámos (we spoke) and falamos (we speak). Since the 1990 agreement, the verb pára is written para, like the preposition, so the accent no longer tells them apart.

examples.note: ends in e, stressed on the last

ptBR.note: In much of Brazil the strong r is an h-like sound (rato ≈ “hatu”) and r at the end of a word is often said strongly.

rules.title: r and rr
rules.text: A single r between vowels, or after a consonant like p, t, b, is one quick tap of the tongue tip behind the top teeth: caro, para, obrigado. A strong r is said at the back of the mouth, like the French r: at the start of a word, after n, l, s, and when written rr: rato, carro, honra. The difference matters: caro (expensive) and carro (car) are different words. At the end of a word the r is weak: falar, mulher. Some speakers in Portugal use a rolled r for the strong one; both are fine.

ptBR.note: In most of Brazil s before a consonant and at the end of a word is a plain s: “mas” is “mas”, “português” ends in s. In Rio it is sh, as in Portugal.

rules.title: s and z as sh: the Portuguese “shh”
rules.text: In Portugal an s before a consonant or at the end of a word sounds like sh: mas “mash”, os pais “oosh paish”, festa “feshta”, português “portoogesh”. Before the voiced consonants b, d, g, m, n, l, r, v it sounds like the s in “measure”: mesmo “mezhmu”, desde “dezhd'”. A final z is also sh: luz “loosh”, vez “vesh”. This sound is very frequent, and learners who say a clear s often sound Spanish or Italian. At the start of a word, before a vowel, s is still s: sol, sábado.

rules.title: s, ss, ç, c and z between vowels and at the start
rules.text: A single s between two vowels buzzes like z: casa, mesa, coisa. ss, ç, and c before e or i are a sharp s: passo, aço, cidade, cedo. At the start of a word s is sharp, and z is a buzz (zero, zona). So casa (house) and caça (hunt) are different words, and so are asa (wing) and assa (he bakes). c before a, o, u is k: casa, copo. ç never comes before e or i: always before a, o, u: açúcar, coração.

rules.title: j, and g before e or i
rules.text: j, and g before e or i, are the s of “measure” or the g of French “genou”: a buzzing sh. It is not the j of “jam” and not a rasp as in Spanish jota. já, janela, gente, gelo, igreja. g before a, o, u is the g of “go”: gato, amigo, gula. To keep the g hard before e or i, a u is added (and not said): guerra, guitarra.

examples.note: g + r: hard g; j: soft

rules.title: lh
rules.text: lh is one sound: the middle of the tongue presses against the roof of the mouth, as in “million” (but more clearly): filho, olho, trabalho, mulher. It is not l + h and not l + y. Spanish speakers should not say ll as in Spanish “calle” (y-like), and French speakers should not stop at y: the tongue touches the roof of the mouth. Italians find it easy: it is the same as gli in figlio. velho (old) and vela (candle) are different words.

rules.title: nh
rules.text: nh is one sound, like ny in “canyon” or gn in Italian “gnocchi” and French “montagne”: vinho, ninho, tenho, manhã. It is the same sound as Spanish ñ. It is not n + h: say it with the middle of the tongue against the roof of the mouth. vinha (vineyard) and vila (small town) are different words.

rules.title: x: four sounds
rules.text: x has four values, and you learn them with the word. Most common: sh, as in caixa, xadrez, peixe. Also ks in táxi, tóxico; z in exame, exemplo, exército (e + x + vowel, usually); and a sharp s in próximo, máximo, auxílio. There is no simple rule that works for every word, so use a dictionary when you are unsure. At the start of a word x is nearly always sh.

rules.title: Word endings: -l, -r, -z
rules.text: An l at the end of a syllable is dark in Portugal: the back of the tongue is raised and the sound is close to a very short “w”, as in English “full”: azul, papel, alto, mal. It is not the clear l of Spanish or Italian. Final r is very weak (falar, mulher), and final z is sh (luz). Say these endings softly and shortly: a strong, clear final consonant sounds foreign.

rules.title: h is silent
rules.text: You never say the letter h at the start of a word: hoje is “oje”, hotel is “otel”. Start straight on the next vowel. h is also part of three letter pairs, and there it makes a different sound: ch (sh), lh and nh.

rules.title: ch
rules.text: ch is sh, as in “shop”: chave, chá, chuva, achar. It is not the ch of “church”, and it is not a k (that is qu). Spanish speakers: it is the opposite of your ch. chave (key) and cave (cellar) are different words.

rules.title: qu and gu
rules.text: Before e and i, qu and gu have a silent u: que “ke”, aqui “aki”, guerra “gerra”, guitarra “gitarra”. The ü that marked a spoken u was dropped in 1990. Before a and o the u is usually said: quando (kw), quase, água (gw), língua. So you see the pattern in the word, not in a rule: you learn the exceptions with the words (for example cinquenta, where the u is said: kw).

rules.title: Linking words
rules.text: Portuguese flows from word to word with no stop, and in Portugal a final vowel often disappears before a vowel: de amigos is nearly “d'amigos”, a Ana is “anna”. A last consonant is carried on to the next vowel: os amigos sounds like “oz amigos” (the s becomes z), and mais um sounds like “maiz um”. The same final s that is sh before a consonant (os pais) is z before a vowel (os amigos).
